[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: English 'or' is often exclusive ('tea or coffee') and 'and' can join alternatives ('x is 1 and 2' meaning either value). Java rule: || is inclusive (true when either or both operands are true) and && is true only when both operands are true, so x == 1 && x == 2 is always false.
[1] misconception (M) -> NoSingleLogicAnd: wrong rule: & is only a bitwise operator. Right rule: Java also has a & operator, which the book does not use; on boolean operands it is a logical and that always evaluates both operands; logical and is written &&.
[2] misconception (M) -> BooleanPrecedence: wrong rule: a || b && c is evaluated left to right as (a || b) && c. Right rule: && binds tighter than ||, so a || b && c means a || (b && c); with a = true, b = false, c = false the value is true, not false.
[3] misconception (M) -> NestedIfsInsteadOfLogicalOperators: wrong rule: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if. Right rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).
[4] inconsistent_trace (T) -> NoSingleLogicAnd: Points to LT (! first, then &&, then ||; left operand first; right operand of && / || only if needed). Applied unevenly: in one row of a trace the student evaluates the right operand of && although the left was false (or reads || as exclusive when both operands are true) and in another row applies the rule correctly. (here mixing in: "& is only a bitwise operator")
[5] misconception (M) -> SingleAmpersandForAnd: wrong rule: & and | are the same as && and || for conditions, so either can be used. Right rule: && and || skip the right operand when the left decides the result; & and | always evaluate both, which fails when the right side depends on the left (e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1 throws when x is 0).

[0] names_the_element (N): Logical (boolean) operators: && (and), || (or) and ! (not), which take boolean operands and produce a boolean.
[1] states_the_rule (S): a && b is true if both operands are true and false otherwise; a || b is false if both are false and true otherwise; !a is the opposite of a; these definitions are given in full by truth tables.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): ! is applied before && and ||, and && before ||; the left operand is evaluated first, and for && and || the right operand is evaluated only when the left has not already decided the result.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The result is a boolean: with x = 10, x > 0 && x < 10 is false and x < 0 || x > 10 is false; true || anything is true.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): The operators themselves change no variable; any side effect inside the right operand (i++, a method call) happens only if that operand is evaluated.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Combining boolean sub-expressions with &&, || and ! yields another boolean expression, so arbitrarily complex conditions can be built with parentheses.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): && and || are the short-circuit operators: in a guard such as (x != 0 && y / x > 1) the operand order matters, because the right test runs only when the left one allows it.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): Comparisons bind tighter than && and ||, so comparisons are evaluated first and their boolean results are then combined (month >= 1 && month <= 12).
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): ^ on booleans is a further logical operator, true exactly when the operands differ (it equals (a || b) && !(a && b)), but unlike && and || it always evaluates both operands.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): De Morgan's laws rewrite negated && / || expressions: !(A && B) is !A || !B and !(A || B) is !A && !B.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): The operands must be boolean, and the result is boolean; int operands are a compile-time error.
[6] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Used to combine several conditions into one test: a range check (lo <= x && x <= hi), alternatives (x == 0 || y == 0), a guard followed by the real test (i < n && a[i] != 0), or a rule built step by step as in LeapYear.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> NoSingleLogicAnd: Swapping && for || changes the meaning; negating a whole condition requires De Morgan (negate each term and flip the operator); swapping the operands of && or || keeps the truth value but can change which side effects or exceptions occur.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use && and || to combine conditions into a single test, ordering operands so that cheap or protective tests come first; use nested ifs only when the cases need different actions; do not use & and | for conditions.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Conditions are combined with && and ||; & and | evaluate both operands. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Using & or | where the right operand is only safe when the left decides first, e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1 with x == 0 (ArithmeticException) or an out-of-range index; otherwise a silent difference only when the right side has side effects.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: && has higher precedence than ||. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Mixed && and || without parentheses intended to group the || first, e.g. a || b && c meant as (a || b) && c.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Logical operators take boolean operands only. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Applying && or || to int operands (if (x && y) with ints) or writing and/or as words.

Relational operators compare two numbers to give a boolean; logical operators combine booleans into one boolean.
&&, || and ! are the operations defined on the boolean type: they take booleans and give a boolean.
&&, || and ! combine conditions p and q into one larger condition that is still true or false.
De Morgan's laws rewrite expressions built from && , || and !.
^ on booleans is another logical operator, defined by a truth table like &&, || and !: true exactly when its operands differ.
&& and || evaluate their second operand only when the first has not already decided the result (false && x is false, true || x is true).
